gallery.filename: Good Marksmanship and Guts. DA Poster 21-45.jpg
gallery.title: File:Good Marksmanship and Guts. DA Poster 21-45.jpg
gallery.description: Near Fort Phil Kearney, Wyoming, 2 August 1867. The Wagon Box Fight is one of the great traditions of the Infantry in the West. A small force of 30 men on the 9th Infantry led by Brevet Major James Powell was suddenly attacked in the early morning hours by some 2,000 Sioux Indians. Choosing to stand and fight, these soldiers hastily erected a barricade of wagon boxes, and during the entire morning stood off charge after charge. The Sioux finally withdrew, leaving behind several hundred killed and wounded. The defending force suffered only three casualties. By their coolness, firmness and confidence these infantrymen showed what a few determined men can accomplish with good marksmanship and guts.

gallery.filename: The area West of Powder River, including the Little Bighorn River area - a part of the Crow territory, Fort Laramie Treaty (1851).jpg
gallery.title: File:The area West of Powder River, including the Little Bighorn River area - a part of the Crow territory, Fort Laramie Treaty (1851).jpg
gallery.description:
Part of the Fort Laramie Treaty (1851). The definition of the borders of the Crow territory west of Powder River is framed with red. It was during their invasion in this treaty defined native territory of their traditional enemies in the Crow Nation that the Lakotas, Northern Cheyennes and Northern Arapahoes fought a number of the most mentioned battles with the U.S. Army during the 1860s and 1870s: The Fetterman Fight, The Hayfield Fight, The Wagon Box Fight, Bakers Battle at Pryor’s Creek, The Battle of Honsinger Bluff, The Battle of Pease Bottom, The Battle of Powder River, The Rosebud Battle, The Battle of the Little Bighorn River and The Battle of the Wolf Mountains.
Some sources: 
Hoxie, Frederick E.: Parading Through History. The making of the Crow Nation in America, 1805-1935. Page 107.
Medicine Crow, Joseph: From The Heart Of The Crow Country. The Crow Indians’ Own Stories. New York, 1992. Pages xi, 14 and 84.
Bauerle, Phenocia, Cindy Bell, Luelle Brien, Carrie McCleary, Timothy McCleary and Hubert B. Two Leggins: The Apsáalooke (Crow Indians) of Montana. A Tribal Histories Teacher’s Guide. Crow Agency, 2010. Pages 6-8.
White, Richard: The Winning of the West: The Expansion of the Western Sioux in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries. The Journal of American History. Vol. 65, No. 2 (Sep., 1978), pp. 319-343.
Calloway, Colin G.: The Inter-tribal Balance of Power on the Great Plains, 1760–1850. Journal of American Studies. Vol. 16, No. 1 (April 1982). Pp. 25 – 47. Page 46.
Hyde, George E.: Life of George Bent. Written From His Letters. Norman, 1987. Page 347.

Stands In Timber, John and Margot Liberty: Cheyenne Memories. Lincoln and London, 1972. Page 170, note 13

gallery.filename: Plan of Fort Phil Kearny, Wyoming.png
gallery.title: File:Plan of Fort Phil Kearny, Wyoming.png
gallery.description: Plan of the military post Fort Phil Kearny (1866-1868), Wyoming, in Crow territory as put down in the Fort Laramie treaty (1851). Established on July 17 by Colonel Henry B. Carrington and four companies from the 18th Infantry. The fort was placed between Fort Reno southward and Fort C. F. Smith northward in Montana. The three military posts should protect the emigrant route Bozeman Trail against hostile Lakotas and Cheyennes (”Red Cloud’s War”), who recently had taken treaty defined native land from the Crows. For this reason, the Crows sided with the U.S. Army during the conflict. The fort proper was 600 feet by 800. It had rooms for more than 500 men. The palisade of pine trunks, eight feet high, surrounded an area of 17 acres.
